title: Checkpoint: build and measure a baseline
summary: Measured on a 40 query benchmark, dense retrieval beats the Day 8 TF-IDF system by 17.5 points of recall@1 with a confidence interval that does not cross zero. The win is not on the median query, it is that TF-IDF's failures land at rank 25 and rank 40 while the dense model's worst case is rank 5.
html:
Thirteen days of building, and one question outstanding: was any of it worth it? Today that stops being a matter of opinion. You build a baseline, measure it, and get a number that the next eighty-six days have to beat.

What a baseline needs

Four things, and none of them are the model:

  1. A corpus where the answers actually live.
  2. Questions with known answers. Each one labelled with the passage that answers it.
  3. Metrics. Recall@k and MRR (Days 59 and 60 do these properly; today you just use them).
  4. A confidence interval. Yesterday established why. Without one you have a number, not a result.

Notice the model is absent from that list. The harness is the asset. Models get swapped, the harness persists, and every claim you make for the rest of this course runs through it.

The whole harness

Smaller than you would expect. Given the rank your system assigned to the correct passage for each query, the metrics are three lines:

ranks = np.array([...])          # rank of the gold passage, per query

recall_at_1 = (ranks == 1).mean()
recall_at_5 = (ranks <= 5).mean()
mrr         = (1.0 / ranks).mean()

And the part that turns a number into a result:

# 95% CI on mean(a) - mean(b), paired per query
def bootstrap_diff(a, b, n_boot=20000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    d = a - b                                  # per-query difference
    means = np.array([rng.choice(d, len(d), replace=True).mean()
                      for _ in range(n_boot)])
    return d.mean(), np.percentile(means, 2.5), np.percentile(means, 97.5)

Pairing matters. You resample the per-query differences, not the two score sets separately, because both systems answered the same questions and that shared difficulty should cancel. Unpaired comparison throws away the strongest thing you have.

The measurement

I ran the Day 8 TF-IDF system against e5-small-v2 on the same benchmark from yesterday: 40 passages and 40 queries, all storage and distributed systems, deliberately confusable.

system                        recall@1   recall@5      MRR
Day 8 TF-IDF                     0.700      0.850    0.759
e5-small-v2 dense                0.875      1.000    0.920

Then the paired bootstrap, 20,000 resamples over the per-query differences:

recall@1  dense minus TF-IDF:  +17.5 pts   95% CI [+2.5, +32.5]   P(better) = 0.984
MRR       dense minus TF-IDF:  +0.161      95% CI [+0.043, +0.289]  P(better) = 0.996

Compare that to yesterday, where a 5 point difference gave an interval of [-5.0, +15.0] and established nothing. Today's interval does not cross zero. Same 40 queries, same method, and this time the effect is large enough for the test set to see it. That contrast is the most useful thing in this lesson: it is what it looks like when a measurement works, next to what it looks like when it does not.

The tail is the story

The headline number is misleading on its own. Look at where each system actually put the correct passage:

TF-IDF ranks:  1 x28, then 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 12, 14, 25, 40
dense  ranks:  1 x35, then 2, 2, 3, 4, 5

TF-IDF gets 28 of 40 queries exactly right. It is not a bad system. What it does is fail catastrophically when it fails: rank 12, rank 14, rank 25, and one query where the correct passage came dead last out of 40. The dense model's worst case across the whole set is rank 5.

So dense retrieval does not win by being better on the median query. It wins by not having that tail. For a system where k is 5, a rank 40 result and a rank 6 result are identical, both invisible, and the entire difference in answer quality comes from how often you fall off the edge.

Look at what falls off:

tfidf 40, dense 1  |  how do I avoid storing the same block twice?
tfidf 25, dense 1  |  what data structure tells me a key is definitely absent?
tfidf 14, dense 1  |  how does a controller stop one block from wearing out first?
tfidf 12, dense 1  |  how do you avoid replaying the whole log at startup?

The first one answers to a passage about deduplication. The question never says that word. The second wants the bloom filter passage, which says "false positives but no false negatives" and never says "definitely absent". These are Day 3's vocabulary problem, still unsolved by every lexical trick, and solved by the encoder. Seeing the mechanism from Day 9 produce a measured 17.5 point improvement on your own benchmark is different from being told it would.

Where TF-IDF still wins

Three queries, and they are not noise:

tfidf 1, dense 4  |  what is the simpler but more space hungry redundancy scheme?
tfidf 1, dense 2  |  how do I tolerate m failures without storing k full copies?
tfidf 2, dense 3  |  which RAID level tolerates exactly one drive failure?

All three turn on precise, low-frequency terms where an exact match is the signal. "RAID 5" versus "RAID 6" is one character of difference carrying the entire meaning, and a dense vector smooths exactly that kind of distinction. This is the identifier weakness from Day 9, showing up unprompted in a real measurement.

Which is the argument for not choosing. Both systems are right about different queries, the failures barely overlap, and running both and fusing them is Day 33. You now have your own evidence for it rather than an assertion from a blog post.

What the 17.5 points cost

Worth stating plainly, because a baseline that only records quality is half a baseline. TF-IDF needs no model, no accelerator, and about 560 bytes per chunk, and it builds its index in the time it takes to read the corpus once. The dense system needs a model loaded in memory, an inference pass over every chunk at index time and over every query at serving time, and 4,096 bytes per chunk at 1024 dimensions.

That is roughly seven times the storage and a new hard dependency, bought with 17.5 points of recall@1. At 40 passages nobody cares. At 40 million it is a 164 GB index that has to live somewhere, be searched without a linear scan, and be rebuilt whenever you change the model. Which is the entire subject of the phase that starts tomorrow.

What you have at the end of Phase 1

A complete working retrieval system you wrote by hand, a neural upgrade that measurably beats it, a benchmark, and a bootstrap. The last two matter more than the first two. Keep the harness in version control and treat any change that does not move it as unproven.

One honest caveat about your own numbers. A benchmark you wrote yourself, with one labelled answer per query, on passages you chose, is not a neutral instrument. Your questions probably use vocabulary that is closer to the passages than a real user's would be, and your single labels are almost certainly missing other passages that answer just as well. That does not make the measurement useless, it makes it a lower bound with a known bias. Day 57 builds golden sets properly and Day 58 covers exactly how synthetic questions mislead.

Phase 2 starts tomorrow and the subject changes completely. Everything so far compared a query against every passage in a loop. That works at 40 passages and is hopeless at 40 million. Tomorrow: exact kNN, and why it does not scale.
exercise:
1. Build your own 30 question benchmark. Take a corpus you care about, write 30 questions you know the answers to, and record the correct chunk id for each. This is an hour of unglamorous work and it is the highest value hour in the entire course, because every claim you make from here on gets checked against it.

2. Run both systems and bootstrap the difference. Score your benchmark with your Day 8 TF-IDF code and with any sentence-transformers model. Report recall@1, recall@5 and MRR for each, then the paired bootstrap CI on the difference. If your interval crosses zero, your test set is too small to tell them apart, which is itself the finding.

3. Read your own tail. Sort your queries by the rank each system gave the correct chunk and look at the worst five for each. Write one sentence per failure explaining why it happened. That list is a better guide to what to fix next than any general advice, including mine.
